title: Robe Chant
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the robe chant on page one of the chant book, the first text in a plan to work through the book's chants in turn. After a handshake story from a French train station, Nomon goes through the chant line by line with Shohaku Okumura's commentary, finding that the English translation strays from the three names for the robe: liberating, signless, and field. Nomon asks how sewing and wearing a robe could answer suffering, recalling a hungry man whose food went untouched. Nomon closes with Dogen weeping as monks in a Chinese monastery put their robes on their heads, and with the official Soto Zen translation that Okumura never adopted.

sentences.text: Thank you for participating in that ceremony.
I called Mike this afternoon and he was really happy that we were thinking of Barb and him and doing a ceremony for her, and I feel honored that she's watching over my shoulder right now.
She had such a great spirit, Barb Crowley.
She had a lot of health problems, I don't know if she knew that, but she was often uncomfortable and in all kinds of pain and in and out of the doctor all the time.
But she really just stayed somehow cheerful.
Mike said pretty much until the very end, which was quite sudden and unexpected.
I can tell you the medical story if you're curious.
He told me pretty much the whole story.
Hopefully I can remember it.
It's interesting that we want to know this story so much, don't we?
It's interesting.
So tonight we'll start a little project, keep ourselves out of trouble.
We have this book with lots of different texts in it, which come from somewhere, presumably.
It must have come from somewhere.

What we thought we'd do is start on page one, and eventually, in some distant time, if we're all still alive, we'll make it to page 28 and have talks by me and the other teachers on these different texts.
And in case you didn't know, the little chant we did right before the talk is in here.
It's on page three.
So it'll be like January or something.
Tonight I thought we'd start with the very first text in here.
The robe chant is labeled.
Well, ritual can do a lot for us.
We just did a ritual.
Ritual can slow us down, put us in contact with some feeling for the situation that maybe we weren't so connected with before.
Ritual can remind us of some meaning.
Even if we can't exactly describe it or put a finger on it, there's a feeling to ritual.

And in our Western, postmodern secular discourse, we have the idea that doing ritual without understanding it, or doing it in a rote way, is stale and kind of useless, which is maybe part of our inheritance from the various Western intellectual renaissances, and maybe a kind of shadow of the French Revolution, I was thinking this afternoon.
Down with ritual, down with everything.
Only rationality.
Liberté.

But in my experience, and maybe yours too, ritual action has a power and an impact even when we're not particularly liking it, when we're not particularly paying attention, distracted by something else.
There's something that happens in our body and in our heart when we do ritual practice, especially doing ritual practice with others, which is part of our grand design in Soto Zen.
And if you think about it, our lives are actually full of ritual.
Some of the ritual is just so normal that we don't even notice we're doing ritual.
Shaking hands with somebody is a ritual.
Why do we do that?
What does that ritual accomplish?
What are we supposed to be feeling when we do the ritual of shaking hands?
And it's interesting that in our particular culture or subculture, we usually shake hands the first time that we meet somebody, but only the first time.
Have you noticed that?
When we run into somebody again, meet them for the second time, it's a little bit awkward, like it'd be kind of dorky to shake their hands.
You're sort of stuck in between giving them a hug and smiling and looking off to the side and trying to negotiate with them what the right kind of physical contact or non-contact is.
So we have this ritual and then we have a kind of gray area in our ritual.
We don't know what to do, because maybe that ritual is slowly changing in our culture.
In other parts of the country, you would shake hands every time you meet somebody, even an old, old friend.

I was remembering one time I was in France, and there, if you approach a group of men especially, maybe you've experienced this in other countries too, it's a very important ritual to shake everybody's hand in the group or in the whole room.
You move around the room and you shake everybody's hand before you go on to anything else.
One time I was at the train station and I had to ask the railway official a question.
I think it was probably about getting our bikes onto the train, which was confusing, and the rules were different every time.
The train conductor guy was surrounded by three or four other men.
So I was gonna go ask him, but it was clear I had to shake everybody's hand first.
Me, a stranger, not particularly speaking their language.
But there was a real warmth and connection, and it was really a lovely moment, actually.
I was quite amazed.
I was just kind of uptight and worried about our bikes, and suddenly I was invited into fraternité.
I don't know how I managed to ask my question, because I don't really speak French, but somehow we got through that.
And of course, there are other rituals, meaning a woman in France, you kiss on both cheeks, and some men that you're close to, you would kiss.
So we have many rituals in Zen practice.
Because they are newer to us, they feel a little different from the rituals we don't even notice we're doing.
Here we notice: wow, we're doing ritual.
And these rituals elicit a feeling, or maybe plant something in our hearts for later.
One of our most beautiful rituals is very odd.
It's the putting on of formal robes.
When we say robes, there are different kinds of robes.
There are sitting robes like this, or Kate and Talus have on sitting robes.
Those are not put on with any particular ritual, you just put them on.
They're optional here, worn by people who choose to wear them, which is fine, and not wearing them is fine.
They're kind of nice, though, when you get used to them.
Very practical, actually designed for sitting.
But there are also ritually important robes, robes with religious meaning that are worn on the outermost layer.
In this case, this brown robe is a ritual robe, and the bib-like robe that several people are wearing is a ritual robe.
And there's a ritual for putting on a ritual robe.
You wouldn't just put it on.
Buddhist clergy especially always wear a ritual robe when they practice, and in some contexts wear those robes all the time when they're awake.
It's very complicated, and we're doing a very simple version of this.
In addition to the ritual robe, there are three or four or five layers that you wear underneath.
Each layer has to be tied in the correct way and be the correct color and the correct cut of cloth.
And there's a great big deal made about how long the sleeves are.
These are not really quite big enough, actually.
When a group of everyday Zen priests went to Japan, we had to go through extensive consultation with people in the know to make sure that we wouldn't be too far out of whack with our clothing.
And probably still we didn't have it quite right.
But we were guests, so it's okay.
This larger robe is called Kesa, or O-Kesa, which is a Japanese way of saying Keshia.
And the smaller robe is called rakusu.
So why would you care?
Well, because these rituals have a deep meaning in the tradition.
It's somehow a meaning that we're carrying forward for thousands of years.
And right now we have people creating these robes.
In our tradition, we sew the outer ritual robe ourselves.
I sewed this myself, with lots of help.
And we have some people in the Sangha sewing the smaller robe in preparation for receiving it in another ritual.
There's a pattern on the robes, too, a system of rectangles, which it's hard to see because of the color.
But you should look carefully sometime at the pattern.
The pattern on the robes is said to be the pattern of rice fields.
There's a beautiful story of the Buddha and his attendant walking up a little hill somewhere.
The Buddha looks down at the paths and the rice paddings and says, well, that's really beautiful and important.
Growing rice in Asia is a very important thing.
It's like bread, maybe, for Northern European culture.
So the Buddha looked at the pattern and said, well, let's make our robes in that way, because we're also trying to grow something very important in our practice.
I don't actually know if they grow rice in Northern India at that time.
It might be that this was a Japanese reinterpretation of what happened, who knows.
So we have layers of meaning and change also in our rituals.
Our rituals are changing.
When this robe is put on for the first time, usually in the morning, it's actually put on top of the head.
Before it's put on, you put it on top of the head and you do a special chant.
The top of the head, in Chinese culture, I guess, is a very vulnerable place where you put something very special, which is a little different for us, I guess.
In our particular range of weekly practices here, we do this ritual on Saturday mornings at six in the morning, every Saturday morning, pretty much at six in the morning.
There are people in this very room putting things on top of their heads and doing a special chant.
Really beautiful.
So you must make it down here at least once for that.
Even if it's not your favorite to be up at six in the morning on Saturday, you should come sometime.
It's really beautiful.
The idea is that the first time you put the ritual robes on for the day, you would do this chant, this ritual.
Lately I've been wondering if we should do that at the beginning of our Wednesday night practice, because probably few of us have put the robe on earlier that day.
We can talk about that sometime.
Doing the ceremony in the early morning is a reference to the daily routine in the Zen monasteries all over the world.
Every morning in all the Zen monasteries, the monks and nuns are doing this ritual in the dark, very mysterious.
This morning at Tassajara Zen Mountain Center in California, our members Chris and Edie did that ritual, put their okesa on top of their heads and chanted this chant.
And they'll do so tomorrow and the next day and every day till they leave there in December.
So let's look at page one, and we will chant the robe chant.
Not all of us know it, so we'll do it a little different from usual.
We'll do call and response.
I'll chant it so you can hear the pronunciation and the pattern.
I'll do a line and then we'll all do a line together, and then I'll do the next line, okay?
So listening first.
But you can look with your eyes too.
Listen and look.
I just found out today the title of this chant in Japanese is ta-kei-sa-gei.
So that was the ta-kei-sa-gei.
Didn't know that till today.
So what language is this that we're actually chanting?
You might wonder.
These mysterious sounds.
Maybe ritual is more powerful when we don't know what it means.
Maybe I'm going to mess it up.
So what language is this?
That's a whole Dharma talk in itself, because it's a strange blend of languages.
The best name for this language is Sino-Japanese.
What it is is the way the Japanese pronounce Chinese characters when they're referring to them as Chinese instead of referring to them as Japanese.
In the case of referring to them as Japanese, they have a different pronunciation.
And on the page we don't have Chinese characters.
We have Roman letter transliterations of the sounds they're making, using the Japanese range of sounds.
So it's a little inaccurate to say it's Japanese.
We say that, but it's not quite accurate.

The funny thing is that a modern, well-educated Japanese person going into a Zen temple for the first time and being handed the chant book with the Chinese characters would not know how to pronounce it.
Some of the characters are archaic and not used in modern Japanese, and the rest of them, which might be used, they would know a different pronunciation.
They might know a few of them, but probably not all of them.
Sometimes they add other little teeny letters using the Japanese phonetic alphabet, which looks totally different, as little hints for how to pronounce it.
So it may seem strange to you, and you might think, well, a Japanese person would know what this means.
No.
There are these layers of history of a culture coming from one place to the next that's embedded in these sounds.
So that's interesting, huh?
A little obscure and strange.
So what does this actually mean?
We have a translation in English below here.
*Great robe of liberation, field far beyond form and emptiness.
Wearing the Tathagata's teaching, saving all beings.*
There's a technical word in there, Tathagata, which is one of the many words for Buddha.
I want to give a little more information about that translation, and not because I learned all the characters.
I can more or less look up characters, which takes me a really long time.
But a wonderful Japanese teacher wrote a book about most of the short chants in our chant books, so we have a great source.
Each person who gives a talk is going to sound really smart thanks to this book.
So we'll know better.
This is by Shohaku Okumura, who's a Japanese-trained Zen priest who lives in Bloomington, Illinois, and has a center there.
He might be one of the best-trained Zen priests in the world, actually.
There he is in Illinois with a little center out of his house.
Zendo's in the garage.
Just a few students.
So it's interesting.
So here it is.
Here the letters, you might need to move a little bit, and if you can't see, feel free to move, are arranged actually in how the words go.
Ours is arranged more or less for chanting.
So each of these is a word.
So dai, and I won't attempt a few of these.
I know the characters, but I usually make them wrong, so I won't even try.
Dai just means great.
So far so good.
And sai doesn't have a meaning.
It's kind of like an aspirant.
It's like an exclamation mark.
So this first part is like, great!
Or how great.
That's pretty good.
Gei da fuku.
Gei da fuku.
Excuse me, gei da fuku.
The line means, hold the sound longer.
It's the first of three names in here for the robe.
So that's also interesting about Buddhism and probably most religious traditions: that meaning is slippery, right?
Meaning is slippery.
And so just one word won't quite capture the meaning.
So often in Buddhist texts they have long, long lists of synonyms and multiple different words for one thing.
And we saw this the other day when we studied the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines.
So what we're about to encounter are actually three different names for this robe.
And the first one is the most straightforward.
Gei da fuku means robe, liberating robe, or robe of liberation.
So the first line is a pretty good translation.
But then we start to get into a little bit of difficulty.
It turns out our translation is wrong.
Which is also interesting, right?
Can things be right or wrong?
If something got changed by somebody, was it changed for good reason?
Should we change it back?
Should we keep it?
So muso means no sign.
No sign.
It's a transliteration of a Buddhist term that means signless.
So not having a mark or distinguishable stable characteristic.
It's a synonym for emptiness, if you study the teachings on emptiness.
But the most direct translation is signless.
And the idea there is that when we see things and ascribe meaning to them, we're not really seeing the whole thing.
We're just seeing some sort of sign or some aspect of it.
Then we assume there's a whole other thing there.
And the idea here is that the actual nature of things is they don't really have that.
We see some little element of it and we assume all kinds of stuff.
So this is saying that the robe actually is signless.
It's beyond any sort of conceptual holding down.
So we don't have signless, or we do have emptiness, at the end of our first line in English.
We have "field, far beyond form and emptiness."
So fukkadenne means, fukkadenne means...
I also got a little bit scrambled up, excuse me a minute.
Fukkadenne.
So this actually does: fuku does make field.
This means a field.
Denne means something like liberation or freedom.
So a field of freedom, let's say.
Or it could be a field of liberation.
Let's say freedom, because I think it's closer to that.
So it's actually a great robe with three different synonyms.
It's a liberating robe, it's a signless robe, and it's like a field.
And agrarian metaphors are common in Buddhism.
We have Buddha fields, we have the ground of being, we have lotus flowers and things growing.
So it's all sort of metaphorical language.

But our translation, "field, far beyond form and emptiness," is a little bit problematic, because the word for emptiness is not really here, although there's a synonym, and the word for form is not here at all, whatsoever.
And this idea of a field that's beyond form and beyond emptiness, Shohaku Okumura in his book says, I don't know what that means.
I don't know how there could be a field beyond form and emptiness.
And it sounds really cool, but what does it mean?

So what it appears to be is that whoever translated this into English in the 1960s or something saw that there's some element of a field and some element of emptiness or signlessness or formlessness, and just jumped into another important text, which we'll talk about later, the Heart Sutra.
It talks about a kind of interpenetration between the form that something seems to be taking and its actual nature as shifting and empty and not really that fixed.
So they seem to have done a big leap into the Heart Sutra, which actually isn't in the text.
So here we have just a list of qualities of the robe.
So the next line: ibu is a very straightforward verb, and it means to unwrap, to unfold, to open.
Let's say unfold.
And that's a reference to how you put this thing on, actually.

What you do is you fold it up in a particular way, and after you put it on your head, you put it on your shoulder and you go through this complicated, sneaky way of unfolding it and wrapping it around your body.
So, unfolding.
And unfolding has a lot of meanings, right?
How do we unfold things?
How do we open things?
Things seem to be compressed, and when things are folded, they're hidden in a certain way, right?
Most of the surface is hidden.
So how can we live a life of unfolding?
And nyorai is the word for Buddha.
It's a totally irregular word for Buddha.
And there's a bunch of different Buddhas, and which Buddha it is is not specified.
We assume it's Shakyamuni Buddha, the main historical Buddha, who in Japanese is Sakya.
Sakya.
I'm forgetting.
Sakya nyorai.
Sakya nyorai.
And kyo is like do, the way.
So it's the Buddha way.
So somehow putting on this robe is a way of unfolding the Buddha way.
So our line, "wearing the Tathagata's teaching," is not too bad.
But the word teaching is implied by way.
It's not really there.
And it doesn't say wearing.
So I don't know if it's good to dig into this.
That's going to bother us every time we chant it.
But that's human, right?
And the last line, I cease sounding super smart because I couldn't find a character-by-character translation.
This book is actually not carefully written essays.
It's talks.
Like most Buddhist books are talks, actually.
I ever wonder how can these people write so many books?
They don't.
They give lots of talks.
And they have really loyal students who transcribe them and edit them into books.
So Shohaku that night must have just gone somewhere else and never quite finished the job.
But all the translations that I've seen make it sound like this is a pretty straightforward expression.
Ours has "saving all beings."
Other translations say "freeing all beings."

So it's something along those lines: that the great robe, which is signless and like a field, like being in a field or lying in a field, being wrapped in a field, allows the possibility of unfolding the Buddha way.
And the purpose of that is to free and liberate and help other beings.
So why would you make such a big deal about fabric?
Sewing and wearing special clothing.
And how could that be saving anybody?
That seems, on the face of it, maybe a little precious.
And the kind of thing that people dislike about religion.
I suppose it could be, if that's our only response to suffering, putting on special clothing.
Maybe we're not helping.
We definitely should also respond in practical ways.
If someone's hungry, give them food, right?
Simple.
And yet not so simple.
I sometimes tell the story: one time we were doing a retreat at the previous Dharma hall down the way, a block, and I went on a walk.
Now there's condos there, but kind of down where some of the apartments are, and below the bridge, and I found a hungry person who was blathering and confused, and he fell down.
I helped him up, and it seemed like he needed food.
It was the break from the retreat and I was all fired up, because we were doing our meditation thing.
So I dashed home, got food I thought he would like, and came back and gave it to him, and had a weird conversation.
I didn't understand what he was saying.
And I went back later and the food was not touched.
So it seems simply doing practical things, [unclear: "Can't quite say beans either"].
So it might be that we need to do practical things with some deep feeling.
Some sense of the underlying fabric of the universe, if you will, or it just doesn't work out.
And maybe this is the wisdom of Prajnaparamita informing the other five Paramitas that we studied the other day.
So we put on the robe and we engage in our deep ritual life as a way to touch the depth of our human experience.
And so actually it's not just sitting around doing something for fun or because we have some pride or something like that.
It's a very serious response to suffering.
Wearing the robe is wrapping the world in healing and teaching.
And the whole system that's constellated around the robe and supported by it requires a lot of us.
It requires commitment, as perhaps you've noticed.
When you walk in the door here, I think you can feel, wow, a big commitment place.
I don't know, they're nice, but I don't know if I'm up for this.
And we actually have three people now trying to sew the small robe for the Jukai Precepts Receiving Ceremony, which will happen in the middle of November.
Hope you can come.
And maybe you remember that I talked about this earlier, and at one point there were six people sewing the robe.
And now there are three, and we'll see how many there are at the ceremony.
And there's no problem with that, but it just shows you it's a hard thing to do.
It takes a lot.
It takes a lot of alignment from the whole universe, it takes a lot of support, and it takes a lot of individual commitment, and it takes a lot of help.
And this may make it sound like the only useful way to practice here would be to get on the fast track, learning about this robe thing and what do you have to do to get that done.
But we don't see it that way.
The way we see it is that some people are called to express the wearing of the robe in that very tangible way.
Other people wear the robe in other ways, taking care of their life as ritual, as a deep engagement with the world, whether they're wearing obvious robes or not.
Doing other jobs around the temple or other things in their lives.
And those of us who wear the physical robe are not doing it for ourselves.
We're doing it for everybody.
So we will do this for you.
You don't have to do it.
And we'll chant this chant with a feeling for its meaning, maybe, and a feeling that's beyond meaning.
Because it's not just about what we can talk about.
There's a deep feeling to all of this.

So the founder of the school of Zen, Eihei Dogen, wrote in his journal about going to China in 1222 or so, that he finally got admitted into one of the monasteries after much trouble and drama, which he doesn't really write about, but historians have figured out that it was probably really hard for him to get into the monastery.
And he woke up the first morning at 3 in the morning, or whenever they woke up, dark and mysterious.
And the monks, probably it was all monks, put their robes on their heads and chanted this very chant, or some other pronunciation of it probably.
And Dogen was really impressed.
He wrote:
*When I saw this I rejoiced, tears wetting my robe.
Although I knew this verse, I had not seen the way it was done, and now I saw with my own eyes.
And in my joy I felt so sad and sorry that there had been no master to teach this to me, no good friend to recommend it to us in Japan.
How sad that so much time had been wasted.
My sadness and joy brought endless tears.*
In his writings now we think of him as very smart and obtuse, and kind of a tough old guy.
But here he was crying away as a young man in a foreign country, you know, what was going on, and watching them chant and put their robes on their heads.
So it's a very big deal for him.
It's a big deal for us now.
And even if you don't go through all this stuff that you'd have to do to wear one for yourself, as I was mentioning, please don't feel bad or like you're not fully practicing.
We'll wear the robe for everyone.
And one thing that's interesting too in the story of this translation is the great conservatism of religion that's in evidence here.
Because Shohaku Okumura, who pointed out the problems in this translation to us, speaks very good English and figured out that especially the second line is quite off.
And it's the English translation that he also received when he took over the Zen Center of Minneapolis in about 1980, when the previous teacher there, Katagiri Roshi, was dying.
And then when Shohaku went on to start his own place in Illinois, he kept the same English translation.
Didn't change it.
And certainly he could have.
He was as empowered as anybody to do his own thing, to make up his own translation.
And there's even an official translation from the central Zen, Soto Zen organization, which is much closer to his understanding of the characters.
It goes like this:
*How great the robe of liberation, a formless field of merit.
Wrapping ourselves in Buddha's teaching, we free all living beings.*
So I just find it interesting that Shohaku didn't change to that or some other version of that.
He stuck with what he had been taught by one of his teachers.
Maybe it will be some generations before we decide to revise the English.
So, a little talk.
I hope that wasn't too technical, kind of interesting, on the robe chant.
Thank you for listening to that, and thank you for helping us to celebrate, with a little ritual, the life and the passing of Barb Crowley.
I also want to mention that I have here for us a letter from Chris Burkhart, one of the people doing the robe chant at Tassajara.
A nice long handwritten letter.
They're keeping letter writing alive.
It's the other tradition they're keeping alive at the Zen monastery, because not a lot of [unclear: "deaf computers"].
There's one telephone, I guess, but you can't really access it, so you write letters.
I'll bring this up to the lobby.
You can read it.
*May all beings feel and understand that we're all being wrapped in the comfy embrace of Buddha's robe.*
